extracted.intended_audience: artists, art students, critics, and readers interested in forming or judging aesthetic taste
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for cultivating, judging, and producing works of art grounded in reason, common feeling, historical study, and a balance of essential principles and ornaments. Emphasizes observing human nature, studying past masters and sister arts, and tempering innovation with prevailing prejudices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste and reason are connected
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject the notion that 'taste and genius' have nothing to do with reason; taste must be subject to rational judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason ought to preside from first to last in artistic invention; philosophy and rules do not stifle imagination but give 'manly confidence' and prevent vain presumption. Anti-pattern: celebrating inventions that 'disdain or shrink from reason' as true genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not take particular living objects for nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid treating particular living individuals as if they are the standard of Nature; art should not merely copy particular examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The imagination 'can only vary and combine these ideas with which it is furnished by means of the senses' — aim at the general idea of nature rather than slavish portraiture of particulars. Anti-pattern: literalism that mistakes singular instances for the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to common sense and general feelings of mankind
rubrics_metrics.description: Taste and the principles of imagination should be established by an 'appeal to common sense deciding upon the common feelings of mankind.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the uniform and agreed feelings of people as the standard for what pleases; test artistic effects against common human affections rather than private eccentricities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality / public concurrence as a test
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of a general uniformity in human minds, rules of art are justified by what has pleased various ages and countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works that have pleased different ages/places and continue to please are likely to please again; use public reception and historical persistence as evidence of true merit. Anti-pattern: valuing only what pleases a single age, nation, or clique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination recombines sensory material, not absolute originality
rubrics_metrics.description: The imagination is 'incapable of producing anything originally of itself' and must vary and combine sensory ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value originality of combination and judgement over fanciful claims to wholly new forms. Ground invention in sensible materials and shared ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulate affections by the responses of others
rubrics_metrics.description: Our affections and judgements must be regulated by those of others; a well-disciplined mind 'submits its own opinion to the public voice.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test effects on a broader audience rather than relying on solitary approval; beware of resisting authority in a way that opens one to 'singularity, vanity, self-conceit.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquire knowledge of human dispositions by experience and observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge of how imagination and passions operate is gained by experience—examining oneself and, crucially, confirming sensations by wider observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with introspection to suggest inquiries, but verify by observing others across contexts. Scoring note: claims about human response that lack corroboration by observation are weak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study works across ages, countries, and arts
rubrics_metrics.description: Familiarity with works that have pleased different ages and nations supplies more materials for judging what is analogous to the mind of man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broaden reading and viewing beyond one's immediate time/place; interhistorical and intercultural knowledge strengthens judgement. Examples: learn from Greek and Roman models as well as modern masters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use analogy between the arts (cross-disciplinary learning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many principles are ascertained by analogy—one art can suggest discoveries in another; arts address the same faculties via different media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Borrow and test practices across sister arts when appropriate (e.g., rhetorical devices illuminating painting). Anti-pattern: rigidly siloed practice that ignores useful analogies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish fixed (natural) principles from fluctuating fashions
rubrics_metrics.description: Every art has both 'fluctuating as well as fixed principles'; it is necessary to determine which are enduring and which arise from custom or habit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize principles grounded in human nature and long durability; treat fashions and accidental associations as secondary. Use tests (see 'translation/durability') to classify elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test truth/wit by translatability and durability
rubrics_metrics.description: A test for whether wit or beauty is genuine: whether it 'preserves itself when translated' and survives across languages/ages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an effect or wit depends only on one language/culture, it is likely local or false; prefer elements that sustain themselves over time and place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornaments are secondary but essential to character
rubrics_metrics.description: Ornaments (colouring, figurative expressions, metre, dress) are not the substantial beauties but give peculiar character and complexion to an art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate ornaments because they contribute to immediate effect and national character, but do not mistake them for the lasting principles of art. Example: verse metre distinguishes poetry fundamentally, though specific metres vary by custom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderate use of figurative and metaphorical language
rubrics_metrics.description: How far figurative or metaphorical language may proceed, and when it becomes affectation, must be determined by taste regulated by the presiding feelings of mankind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid excessive or turgid metaphorical language; balance ardour with chasteness according to audience and established standards. Anti-pattern: language considered 'turgid and inflated' by some cultures while lauded as majestic by others—use taste to mediate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect prevailing prejudices and custom when reforming taste
rubrics_metrics.description: One cannot reform a nation's taste by directly attacking prevailing prejudices; reformation must be gradual because 'Men's minds must be prepared to receive what is new.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When innovating, yield somewhat to preconceptions and introduce change incrementally. Example: a radical Roman manner displeased Venetian eyes accustomed to richness; reform requires time and preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider material durability and longevity in judgements
rubrics_metrics.description: Durability of materials (e.g., in architecture vs dress) often contributes to superiority and lasting prejudice in favour of certain works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for the physical permanence of an artwork's materials when assessing lasting value—longer-lasting materials often aid enduring reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt representation to audience prejudices while preserving likeness
rubrics_metrics.description: In portrait painting one should dignify a subject by aligning some aspects (dress, air) with general prejudices about dignity while retaining modern likeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance antiquarian/learned forms and contemporary truth to satisfy both public expectation and fidelity. Anti-pattern: refusing to respect public prejudices (e.g., an entirely naked statue of Voltaire) leading to rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy and critical study enhance taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy 'gives knowledge' and substitutes rational firmness for presumption; great imaginative names (Plato, Aristotle, Horace, Boileau, Pope) combined genius with critical skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study principles and the conduct of masters; critical reflection and philosophical study will strengthen, not weaken, creative powers. Scoring note: inventive works lacking critical grounding may be judged as 'dreams of a distempered brain.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral character influences sound taste
rubrics_metrics.description: It is often observed that 'the good and virtuous man alone can acquire this true or just relish' for works of art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate moral habits of mind—the same search for truth in serious life transfers to the pursuit of beauty; virtue supports steadiness, durability and preference for substantial excellences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the quasi-natural basis of secondary truths
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary or apparent truths (prejudices, fashions, associations) though local and temporary still have a foundation 'however slender' in the original fabric of our minds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give weight to secondary truths in proportion to their stability and influence; they deserve attention but must not override immutable principles. Use reason to 'regulate' lesser prejudices in favour of more durable ones.
